role: The second reading: each entry read to refute it, not to admire it.
method: Each fragment read whole beside what show.cjs prints for the grape (GRAPES_PLUS and GRAPES, TASTE, INTRO_GRAPES, GRID_SAY, GRID_READS, the service rows) and beside the Codex's region records for Salta and Argentina, Santorini and Greece, Tokaj, Somló and Hungary, the Jura, South West France, Virginia and the Txakoli country, with the service reference and the pairing data where they name the wine.

Every fact the reviewed records do not already state was put to search: the parentage of Torrontés and what grows in Chile and Uruguay, the styles of Torrontés that are not dry, the rules of Santorini, Nykteri and Vinsanto, Tuscan Vin Santo, the own rooted vines, the Clare Valley, the ranking of Tokaj and the reform of 2013, the date of dry Furmint, Šipon, Tokay and Tocai, the kinship of Savagnin and Sauvignon Blanc, the service of vin jaune, Heida, the Australian vines, the Jurançon rule, the parentage of Petit Manseng, the tale of Henri IV and Petit Manseng in Virginia.

The glass read as a blind taster would: each note asked whether a taster would nod, each prose field scanned by a script for a family word in disguise, each ladder set beside the Codex's own climate line for the place, and each tell checked against the entry's own notes, so that no tell parts two grapes by a note both carry.

All five are home grapes, so there is no side by side to test: each home and abroad pair was read for a false or lazy generalisation and against TASTE.world (new for Torrontés, old for the other four), and no question carries a worlds tag.

The four lines counted and said aloud for the five beats in order and for a pronoun that lands on the wrong thing; the sale read for its two sentences and for whether it is said to a guest; the cards and questions read for one key, four options of one kind and a stem that gives nothing away; the compare tells read from both sides against every fragment written so far that names these grapes.

node .scripts/grapes/build-grapes.cjs --lint --chunk g6 run after every round of edits until it printed five of five sound. The writing build was never run and no file but the five fragments and this record was touched.
limits: This session reached search alone. Three source hosts were tried and none resolved (winesofgreece.org, bor.hu, swisswinevalais.ch), so no further host was tried: a page is cited as search results quoted it, and every address the authors gave stays unconfirmed.
The brief allows five searches a grape. Torrontés took three, Assyrtiko four, Furmint four, Savagnin four and Petit Manseng four.

Where a source's address names a person or a producer it is left out and the fact is cited from another page (several study pages on Santorini and Tokaj, and the reports that name the Clare Valley grower).
The Chardonnay, Riesling, Albariño, Chenin Blanc, Sémillon and Viognier entries do not name these grapes, so those tells were read from one side only.

torrontes.verdict: Sound after nine fixes. The parentage, the three varieties, the unrelated vine of Galicia, the pergola and the pisco of Chile were confirmed; two absolutes about sweetness, one of geography and one tell were wrong or loose.
tested: say against GRID_SAY (tor-ron-TES): the same, and right, with the stress on the last syllable as the accent shows.

Parentage: Torrontés Riojano as a natural cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica (the mission grape, Listán Prieto), on the microsatellite study of 2003 as two general references report it. Torrontés Sanjuanino has the same parents and Mendocino has Muscat of Alexandria and an unknown second parent, so three varieties stands, and Riojano is the most perfumed of them.
The Torrontés of Galicia as an unrelated vine: confirmed, and it is the Codex own line in the Ribeiro record.

Abroad: Chile and Uruguay grow it, and much of Chile goes to pisco. Confirmed in general sources. Which Torrontés Chile grows is disputed (Riojano in one, Sanjuanino as Moscatel de Austria in another, a separate Torontel in a third); the entry rightly does not say.

The label words. Cosecha tardía as the one style that is not dry: refuted, since Argentina also bottles sparkling Torrontés, some of it sweet, and a few off dry wines. Valles Calchaquíes with Cafayate at its southern end: refuted by the Codex own Salta record, which runs the valleys on south of Cafayate into Tucumán and Catamarca.

The glass as a blind taster: each note set beside the Court grid read (lemon, lime, orange, peach, apricot, lychee, flowers, bitterness yes) and the reviewed profile (rose, geranium, orange blossom, jasmine, table grape). One published note adds passion fruit. A script found one family word in a sentence (a floral, dry white, in a food line).

The ladder against TASTE (warm) and the grid read (Salta and Mendoza, warm): Cafayate on the warm rung and the upper valley above it on the moderate one agree with the Codex record of the upper valley from about 2,300 metres.

Structure against the reviewed profile (acid medium to medium plus, alcohol medium plus, body light to medium, dry despite the nose): agrees. The grid read puts the acidity a step higher, at medium plus to high.
Home and abroad against TASTE.world (new): the grape is at home in the New World and no Old World style of it exists to set beside it; the mode is right.
Service against the Codex row for light aromatic whites and TASTE.age (the freshest bottle you can find): agree.
The four lines counted (23, 45, 104 and 42 words) and said aloud: the trick first, then home, scent and taste, the cellar, the food, the parentage as the hook. Nothing a guest must have explained.

Compare tells from both sides: the Muscat Blanc and Gewürztraminer entries both write of Torrontés (the grapey nose on a dry frame with a bitter finish; the shared rose perfume, lighter and fresher). The Gewürztraminer tell here gave rose petal to Torrontés alone, against that entry; the Viognier entry does not name Torrontés.
Cards and questions: one key each, four options of one kind (four wines with their origins, four reasons, four pieces of advice), nothing given away; a home grape, so no worlds tag.

The drill. The grape gathers every bank question that names it, and one bank question on Treixadura (c-f5pw6pll) and one region question on Ribeiro name Torrontes in their explanations, meaning the Galician vine.

assyrtiko.verdict: Sound after five fixes. The rules of the protected name, Nykteri, Vinsanto, the own rooted vines and the Clare Valley were confirmed; one absolute about Tuscany was false, the long line could be misheard in two places, and one tell leaned on notes the entry lists as its own.
tested: say against the Codex Greece record (ah-SEER-tee-ko): the same, with the stress on the second syllable.

The 85 per cent floor of dry Santorini. Many pages still print 75. The Codex region record holds that the floor was raised from 75 to 85 by an amendment of 2022, and two sources read give 85; the entry stands with the Codex.

Nykteri: at least three months in oak, confirmed in several sources with a floor of strength the entry does not give. Vinsanto: at least 51 per cent Assyrtiko, sun dried, at least two years in cask, never fortified: confirmed. The drying is 12 to 14 days in most sources, 8 to 14 in one and 5 to 10 in another; the question says a week or two, which holds.

The own rooted vines: the soil of ash, pumice and sand holds almost no clay and phylloxera does not survive in it. Confirmed; one source adds that some credit the vine and not the soil. The kouloura against wind, sand and sun: confirmed, and it is the Codex own trap that the basket does not keep phylloxera away.

Abroad: mainland wines fruitier and milder than the island ones in two sources (one calls them richer and less mineral); the Clare Valley planted in 2012 from cuttings brought from Santorini, with a first wine dated 2014 in one account and 2016 in two. Since the 2010s holds.

The glass as a blind taster: lemon, underripe peach, quince and pith with salt, crushed volcanic rock and beeswax are the reviewed profile; lime, flint and smoke the Régionale row. Orange blossom on the mainland rung sat badly with an entry whose every tell says it has less scent than its neighbours.
The ladder against TASTE (warm) and the Régionale row (warm, island): Santorini on the warm rung, the mainland on the moderate one.
Structure against the reviewed profile (body medium, acid searing, alcohol medium to high, bone dry): agrees.
Service: the row for light aromatic whites, with Nykteri and old bottles a little warmer; TASTE.age (three to eight, longer than its island suggests): agree.

The four lines counted (21, 43, 110 and 37 words) and said aloud. The long line never said the grape was white or Greek, and two of its sentences opened on It with the wrong thing in the ear: the vines, and then Nykteri.

Compare tells: Chardonnay, Riesling and Albariño, as the reviewed confuse line has them. None of those three entries writes of Assyrtiko; the Furmint entry does (saltier and less smoky), which agrees.
Cards and questions: one key each, four options of one kind (four wines with their origins, four ways of making a sweet wine, four purposes), nothing given away.
The guest answer on Vin Santo said neither wine is fortified.

changed.why: Tuscany has a fortified Vin Santo, labelled liquoroso, so neither is fortified is false. The true difference a guest can use is the drying: in the sun on Santorini, indoors in Tuscany.

furmint.verdict: Sound after nine fixes. The ranking of the vineyards, the reform of 2013, the making of Aszú and the names abroad were confirmed; the blind question had two defensible keys, the ladder set Slovenia on the wrong rung, and three lines said a little more than the sources do.
tested: say against the Codex Tokaj and Somló records (FOOR-mint): the same.

Tokaj ranked its vineyards more than a century before Bordeaux: the classing of the sites began about 1730 and was finished by the censuses of 1765 and 1772, with the royal decree of 1737 closing the district; Bordeaux is 1855. Holds on any of the dates.

The reform of the 2013 vintage: three and four puttonyos abolished, every Aszú at 120 grams of sugar a litre or more, six at 150, eighteen months in oak where two years stood before, five and six optional on the label. Confirmed in three sources and in the Codex record. One bottle note read says 130 grams and stands alone.

Dry Furmint since the 1990s, often from a single vineyard. The sources date the single vineyard wines from the 2000 vintage and say dry wine was made before it; the Codex Tokaj record says the 1990s. The answer now gives no decade.

Tokay and Tocai: the European rule of 2007 that kept the name Tokaj for Hungary is confirmed. That neither wine had anything to do with Hungary went past the Codex record, which says neither has anything to do with Tokaj; no source read settles the old tale that Alsace took its vine from Hungary.
Abroad: Šipon in Slovenia, dry by tradition and marked by its acidity; Somló; Rust; Slovak Tokaj. Confirmed, the last three by the Codex records.

The ladder against TASTE (moderate), the Régionale row (cool to moderate) and the Codex records (the cooler north west arm of Tokaj; cool nights and slow ripening on Somló). The moderate rung held Štajerska with ripe pear, quince and apricot, while the entry's own label calls its Šipon taut.

The glass as a blind taster: green apple, pear skin, lime, smoke and flint are the reviewed profile, quince and salt the Codex Tokaj record, saffron, honey and ginger its Aszú. A smoky edge stood as a note with its article on.
Structure against the reviewed profile (body medium, acid high and fiery, dry or lusciously sweet): agrees.

Service: dry Furmint at 10 to 13 degrees Celsius beside the Tokaj record's 10 to 12; Aszú colder, as the service reference row for sweet whites, Tokaji named in it. TASTE.age (dry keeps a decade, Aszú far longer): agrees.

The four lines counted (20, 47, 105 and 43 words) and said aloud. The second sentence of the twenty second line ran to 31 words and five commas; the sale spoke of the guest in the third person and named Aszú with nothing to say what it is.

Compare tells from both sides: Riesling, Chenin Blanc and Assyrtiko, as the reviewed confuse line has them. The tell called Assyrtiko leaner, where its own entry says sturdy, with more alcohol and weight. The Petit Manseng entry writes of Furmint as Aszú and was set right there.

Cards and questions. The blind question listed Assyrtiko of Santorini among its options and put green apple, quince, lime, smoke, flint, a salty finish and fierce acidity in its stem: the Codex gives Assyrtiko lemon, lime, flint, salt, smoke and quince, so two keys could be defended.

changed.was: green apple, quince and lime, a smoky, flinty edge, a salty finish and fierce acidity, with no petrol and no wet wool; options Furmint, Riesling, Chenin Blanc and Assyrtiko of Santorini

changed.why: With salt, lime, flint and smoke in the stem, Assyrtiko of Santorini was a second defensible key. The stem now carries pear skin, which is Furmint's, and shuts out each wrong option by a note it would show.

changed.why: Slovenia's Šipon is dry, neutral to steely and marked by its acidity, and the entry's own label calls it taut; it does not belong on a rung of ripe pear, quince and apricot.

savagnin.verdict: Sound after six fixes. The rule of vin jaune, the clavelin, Château-Chalon, Heida and Païen and the Australian vines were confirmed. One card stated a falsehood: Savagnin is kin to Sauvignon Blanc, most likely its parent.
tested: say against the Codex Jura record (sah-vah-NYAN): the same. The sous voile technique record writes sah-vahn-YAN, the same sounds with the break moved.

The card that called Savagnin no kin of Sauvignon Blanc. Refuted: DNA work reported in two references and by the Swiss wine body shows a parent and offspring tie between the two, with Savagnin taken as the parent because it is the older vine on record; the standard reference work the fragment already cites says the same. The Codex Jura record says only that Savagnin is not Sauvignon Blanc, which is true.

Vin jaune: Savagnin alone, at least sixty months untopped under the veil, sold no sooner than six years and three months after harvest, in the 62 centilitre clavelin, never fortified; Château-Chalon makes nothing else. All of it is the Codex Jura record and its bottle table.

Service: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius on producers' pages and 13 to 15 on the Jura tourism body's; opened an hour to several hours ahead. The entry's 14 to 16 and a few hours ahead stand. The Codex service reference has no row for vin jaune.

Abroad: Heida in the upper Valais and Païen in the lower, the same vine, with citrus, exotic and dried fruit, nuts and honey in the Swiss notes; the Australian vines sold as Albariño and shown in 2009 to be Savagnin, most of them relabelled. Confirmed.
The glass as a blind taster: lemon, green apple, quince and bruised apple, curry, walnut, fenugreek and salt are the reviewed profile. Ripe pear on the Valais rung is in no source read.
The ladder against TASTE (cool): the Jura on the cool rung, the Valais on the moderate one.
Structure against the reviewed profile (body medium to full, acid high, bone dry): agrees.

The four lines counted (24, 47, 109 and 44 words) and said aloud. Left unfilled, the cask grows a veil reads as an empty cask; the sale said the wine tastes like no other white, which the author flagged and which a guest who knows Fino would dispute.

Compare tells from both sides: the Palomino entry writes of Savagnin (unfortified and sharply acid, with walnut and curry, where Fino is lighter, softer and saltier), and the tell here agrees. Chardonnay and Chenin Blanc follow the reviewed confuse line; Gewürztraminer, a candidate of the plan, is kept as kin in a guest answer and a card.
Cards and questions: one key each, four options of one kind (four wines, four statements about the cellar, four accounts of the bottle), nothing given away.
A script found nutty standing for the taste in two prose fields.

changed.was: Savagnin is no kin of Sauvignon Blanc. Whose kin is it? / The Traminer family: it is kin to Gewürztraminer. In the Swiss Valais the same grape is called Heida or Païen.

changed.why: False as written. DNA shows a parent and offspring tie between Savagnin and Sauvignon Blanc, and Savagnin is taken as the parent. The two are different grapes and they are kin.

petit-manseng.verdict: Sound after five fixes. The drying on the vine, the foehn, the late harvest rule, the tale of Henri IV and Virginia were confirmed. One guest answer was wrong (Jurançon is not as sweet as Sauternes, as a rule), and one tell denied the entry a note it lists as its own.
tested: say against the Codex South West France record (puh-TEE mahn-SENG): the same.

The guest answer that Jurançon is as sweet as Sauternes. Refuted for the typical bottle: the specification read sets sweet Jurançon above 40 grams of sugar a litre and the late harvest wine above 55, and the Codex itself calls plain Jurançon off dry in the Court outline and gently to richly sweet in the glass. Sauternes, a fully luscious wine, sits above both as a rule.
Vendanges Tardives: from Petit and Gros Manseng alone, picked from 2 November. Confirmed in the appellation rule as search quotes it.
Passerillage and not noble rot: the thick skins and loose bunches keep rot out, and the same build is why Virginia took the grape up. Confirmed in three sources and the Codex Virginia record.

The tale of Henri IV: born at Pau in December 1553, his lips rubbed with garlic and wet with Jurançon. Told by the regional tourism body and several accounts as a tradition; the entry says they say, and names no one else.

Parentage: an offspring of Savagnin in two references, with Gros Manseng proposed as its own offspring in one and of unknown parentage in another. The entry says only two grapes of the same hills, which holds.

The glass as a blind taster: pineapple, apricot, candied peel, quince and honey are the reviewed profile; the appellation notes read add honey as the mark of the wine, candied and exotic fruit and spice. The tell on Furmint said Petit Manseng has none of the orange peel of Aszú, while candied orange peel stands in this entry's own lead and notes.
The ladder against TASTE (moderate): Jurançon on the moderate rung and Virginia on the warm one, as the Codex Virginia record has it.
Structure against the reviewed profile (body medium to full, acid very high, off dry to sweet): agrees.
Service against the Codex row for sweet whites and TASTE.age (ten and more when sweet): agree.
The four lines counted (21, 43, 110 and 42 words) and said aloud. The long line never said the grape or the wine is white.

Compare tells from both sides: Sémillon as Sauternes, Chenin Blanc of the Layon and Furmint as Aszú. None of those three entries writes of Petit Manseng. The stem of the blind question and one card spoke of the wax of noble rot; wax is Sémillon's, and the entry lists beeswax among its own notes.
Cards and questions: one key each, four options of one kind (four sweet wines, four statements, four grapes), nothing given away.

codexRecords: The Tokaj record (js/regions/hungary.json, tokaj): it dates the dry Furmint of single vineyards to the 1990s, in its history and in its exam line. The sources read date the first single vineyard dry wines to the 2000 vintage and say dry Furmint was made before it. Not shown to be wrong, since the new estates did make dry wine in the 1990s; the table now gives no decade, and the owner may want the record to say the turn of the century.

The Tokaj record against the service reference: Aszú at 10 to 12 degrees Celsius in the region record, sweet whites with Tokaji named at 6 to 8 in js/data-service-ref.js. The table follows the service reference and gives no figure for Aszú. The author's flag, upheld.

The Jura record (js/regions/mapless.json or france.json, jura) and the Savagnin profile say Savagnin is not Sauvignon Blanc and belongs to the Traminer family. True, and it stops short: DNA makes Savagnin a likely parent of Sauvignon Blanc, and of Petit Manseng. The table's card now says so; the record could.
The Jura record respells Savagnin sah-vah-NYAN and the sous voile technique record sah-vahn-YAN: the same sounds, the break moved. The table follows the region record. The author's flag, upheld.
js/data-service-ref.js holds no temperature row for vin jaune; the table gives 14 to 16 degrees Celsius after the Jura's own trade pages, and the region record says cool, not cold.

js/data-questions.js, question c-f5pw6pll (the later ripening native of the Ribeiro, answered Treixadura): its explanation names Torrontes, the Galician vine, so codex53 gathers it into the drill of Argentina's Torrontés by name. The table's notIn now shuts it out, with the Ribeiro region question that does the same. The stem and explanation also write Albarino, Mino and Torrontes without their marks; a frozen bank, so it is only noted.

js/data-grapes-plus.js, the Assyrtiko, Furmint and Savagnin profiles carry words the brief keeps out of a spoken line or a note (saline minerality, phenolic, flor, botrytis spice, curry spice in capitals); the table names sea salt and crushed volcanic rock, a smoky edge, a veil of yeast, saffron and ginger, curry powder and fenugreek.
js/data-intro.js, the Furmint row, calls the grape thin skinned; one source the author read says thick. The table does not say.

The Santorini record gives the floor of dry Santorini as 85 per cent Assyrtiko, raised from 75 by an amendment of 2022. Many pages on the web still print 75. Two sources read give 85; the record is upheld and the table follows it.
unsettled: Whether every source address still answers: none could be opened from this session, and three hosts did not resolve.
Which of Savagnin and Sauvignon Blanc is the parent. DNA shows the tie and not its direction; Savagnin is the older vine on record. The card says a likely parent.
The decade of single vineyard dry Furmint: the Codex says the 1990s, the sources the 2000 vintage. The table gives none.

The residual sugar floors of Jurançon now in force (40 and 55 grams in a specification of 2014 put to the opposition procedure). The table gives no figure and says usually a little less sweet than Sauternes.

Whether Nykteri carries the 85 per cent floor of the dry wine; how many days Vinsanto grapes lie in the sun (12 to 14 in most sources, 8 to 14 and 5 to 10 in others). The table gives no figure for either.
How mainland Assyrtiko differs in the glass: fruitier and milder in two sources, richer and less mineral in one.
Whether Alsace took its Tokay from Hungary, as an old tale has it. The table now says only that neither Tokay nor Tocai had anything to do with Tokaj.
Which Torrontés Chile grows, and the year of the first Clare Valley Assyrtiko (2014 or 2016). The table is silent on both.

Muscat grape under tropical fruit in the Torrontés notes: no family holds it, and the Muscat Blanc entry files its grape under orchard fruit. A family for the grape itself would settle both, if the spec agent ever adds one.
The Wine Spectator address in the Savagnin sources: the fragment's ends 4733, the one search returned here ends 12973.
settled: Torrontés Riojano is a natural cross of Muscat of Alexandria and Criolla Chica; Sanjuanino has the same parents and Mendocino one of them; the Torrontés of Galicia is unrelated.
Argentina bottles sparkling and sweet sparkling Torrontés as well as late harvest wines, so late harvest is not the one style that is not dry.
The Calchaquí valleys run on south of Cafayate into Tucumán and Catamarca.

Nykteri spends at least three months in oak; Vinsanto is at least 51 per cent Assyrtiko, sun dried, at least two years in cask and never fortified; Tuscany has a fortified Vin Santo, labelled liquoroso, and dries its grapes indoors.
Santorini's soil holds almost no clay and phylloxera does not survive in it; the kouloura shelters the fruit and does not keep the pest away.
Assyrtiko was first planted in the Clare Valley in 2012.

Tokaj began classing its vineyards about 1730 and finished by 1772, with the decree of 1737 between; the reform of the 2013 vintage set every Aszú at 120 grams of sugar a litre or more, six puttonyos at 150 and eighteen months in oak, and abolished three and four.
Slovenia's Šipon is dry by tradition and marked by its acidity; Tocai Friulano lost its name in the European Union in 2007.
Savagnin and Sauvignon Blanc are parent and offspring; Petit Manseng is an offspring of Savagnin.
Vin jaune is poured at 13 to 16 degrees Celsius from a bottle opened an hour or more ahead.
Heida in the upper Valais and Païen in the lower are Savagnin; Australia's vines sold as Albariño were shown in 2009 to be Savagnin.
Jurançon Vendanges Tardives is Petit and Gros Manseng alone, picked from 2 November; sweet Jurançon is as a rule less sweet than Sauternes.
Petit Manseng's thick skins and loose bunches keep rot out, in Jurançon and in Virginia.
The tale of the newborn Henri IV, garlic and Jurançon at Pau in 1553 is told as a tradition by the regional bodies.
